subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 8
topic: Electricity · Static charge, current, resistance and circuits · AQA Higher
intro: You may use a calculator. For longer answers write in full sentences and use key words. Describe = say what happens; Explain = say what happens and why (use because and so). 6-mark questions are marked on how well your ideas link together: plan for a minute, then write about 6 linked points. Show your working for calculations and give units. Equations: charge flow Q = I × t; potential difference V = I × R; energy transferred E = Q × V. Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16, Mg = 24. Questions 16 and 17 go back over earlier units.

questions.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. Why?
options: Electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod
Protons moved from the rod onto the cloth
Electrons moved from the rod onto the cloth
The rubbing made new electrons on the rod
questions.ms: B1: electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod. Only electrons move; protons stay in the nucleus, and charge is never made or destroyed.

questions.q: Two balloons are both negatively charged. They are held close together. What happens?
options: They attract
They repel
Nothing happens
They both become positive
questions.ms: B1: they repel. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

questions.q: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp?
options: In series with the lamp
In parallel with the lamp
Next to the battery only
In series with the ammeter
questions.ms: B1: in parallel (across the lamp). Ammeters go in series.

questions.q: Which statement about a series circuit is correct?
options: The current is the same at every point
The potential difference is the same across every component
The current splits between the components
The total resistance is less than the smallest resistance
questions.ms: B1: the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. The potential difference of the supply is shared between the components.

questions.q: What does a diode do?
options: Its resistance falls as the light gets brighter
It only lets current flow in one direction
Its resistance falls as it gets hotter
It stores charge
questions.ms: B1: it only lets current flow in one direction (very high resistance in the reverse direction). The other options describe an LDR and a thermistor.

questions.q: The temperature of a thermistor goes up. What happens to its resistance?
options: It goes up
It goes down
It stays the same
It becomes zero
questions.ms: B1: it goes down. Hotter thermistor, lower resistance (used in thermostats and fire alarms).

questions.q: Explain how rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth makes both the rod and the cloth charged.
questions.ms: B1: friction / rubbing moves electrons from one material to the other (from the cloth to the rod). B1: the object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged (the rod). B1: the object that loses electrons becomes positively charged (the cloth), with an equal amount of charge. Answers that say positive charges / protons move: max 1.

questions.q: A metal dome is charged. Describe what is meant by the electric field around the dome, and how its strength changes with distance.
questions.ms: B1: the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a (non-contact) force. B1: the field is strongest close to the dome and gets weaker further away.

questions.q:
When an aeroplane is refuelled, fuel flows quickly through a rubber pipe from a tanker into the plane.
Explain how static charge can build up during refuelling, why this is dangerous, and how the danger is reduced.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked. Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: the fuel rubs against the inside of the pipe (friction); electrons are transferred between the fuel and the pipe; the plane / tanker becomes charged (one gains electrons, the other loses them); rubber is an insulator so the charge cannot flow away; the charge builds up and the potential difference between the plane and the ground (or the tanker) gets very large; a spark can jump across the gap; the spark can ignite the fuel vapour and cause a fire or explosion; the plane and tanker are connected by a metal earthing / bonding cable (or a conducting pipe is used); electrons flow through the cable to or from the earth, so the charge does not build up and no spark is made.

questions.q: What is an electric current?
options: The rate of flow of electric charge
The energy stored in a battery
The push that makes charge move
The opposition to the flow of charge
questions.ms: B1: the rate of flow of charge. The push is potential difference; the opposition is resistance.

questions.q:
A current of 0.5 A flows through a lamp for 2 minutes.
Calculate the charge that flows through the lamp. (C)
questions.ms: Answer: 60 C. B1 for converting 2 minutes = 120 s. M1 for Q = 0.5 × 120. A1 for 60 C. Using t = 2 (answer 1 C): B0 M1 A0.

questions.q: Calculate the energy transferred when 60 C of charge passes through a component with a potential difference of 12 V across it. (J)
questions.ms: Answer: 720 J. M1 for E = 60 × 12. A1 for 720 J.

questions.q:
A current of 0.5 A flows through a 12 Ω resistor.
Calculate the potential difference across the resistor. (V)
questions.ms: Answer: 6 V. M1 for V = 0.5 × 12. A1 for 6 V.

questions.q:
A potential difference of 6 V across a resistor makes a current of 0.2 A flow.
Calculate the resistance of the resistor. (Ω)
questions.ms: Answer: 30 Ω. M1 for R = V ÷ I = 6 ÷ 0.2 (rearranging V = IR). A1 for 30 Ω.

questions.q:
A 45 Ω resistor has a potential difference of 9 V across it.
Calculate the current through it. (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 0.2 A. M1 for I = V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 45. A1 for 0.2 A.

questions.q:
A student measures the current through a component for different potential differences. The results are in the table.
Potential difference (V)01.02.03.04.05.06.0
Current (A)00.250.400.520.620.700.75

Describe the pattern in the results. Use data from the table in your answer.
questions.ms: B1: as the potential difference goes up, the current goes up. B1: but not in proportion / the current goes up by less each time (the graph would curve). B1 for data, e.g. from 1 V to 2 V the current rises by 0.15 A, but from 5 V to 6 V it rises by only 0.05 A; or doubling 3 V to 6 V does not double the current (0.52 A to 0.75 A).

questions.q: Use the table to calculate the resistance of the component when the potential difference is 2.0 V. (Ω)
questions.ms: Answer: 5 Ω. M1 for R = 2.0 ÷ 0.40. A1 for 5 Ω.

questions.q: Calculate the resistance of the component when the potential difference is 6.0 V. (Ω)
questions.ms: Answer: 8 Ω. B1 for 6.0 ÷ 0.75 = 8.

questions.q: Name the component, and explain why its resistance changes as the potential difference increases.
questions.ms: B1: filament lamp. B1: as the current increases, the filament gets hotter. B1: the ions (atoms) in the metal vibrate more, so the electrons collide with them more often, which increases the resistance.

questions.q:
A 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 12 V battery.
What is the total resistance of the circuit? (Ω)
questions.ms: Answer: 12 Ω. B1. In series, add the resistances: 4 + 8 = 12.

questions.q: Calculate the current in the circuit. (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 1 A. M1 for I = 12 ÷ 12. A1 for 1 A.

questions.q: Calculate the potential difference across the 8 Ω resistor. (V)
questions.ms: Answer: 8 V. M1 for V = 1 × 8. A1 for 8 V. (The 4 Ω resistor gets the other 4 V; the two add up to the battery's 12 V.)

questions.q: Explain why adding another resistor in series makes the current in the circuit smaller.
questions.ms: B1: the total resistance of the circuit increases (resistances in series add up). B1: the battery's potential difference stays the same, so by I = V ÷ R the current is smaller / the charge has to pass through both resistors.

questions.q:
A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel with a 6 V battery. Each resistor is on its own branch.
Calculate the current through the 6 Ω resistor. (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 1 A. M1 for the potential difference across each branch = 6 V and I = 6 ÷ 6. A1 for 1 A.

questions.q: Calculate the current through the 3 Ω resistor. (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 2 A. B1 for 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

questions.q: What is the total current from the battery? (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 3 A. B1. In parallel, the branch currents add: 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.q: Explain why the total resistance of the two resistors in parallel is less than 3 Ω.
questions.ms: B1: adding a second branch gives the charge another path to flow through. B1: so the total current is bigger for the same potential difference, which means the total resistance is smaller (6 V ÷ 3 A = 2 Ω, less than either resistor).

questions.q:
Describe a method to investigate how the length of a wire affects its resistance.
Include the equipment you would use, how you would make it a fair test, and how you would use your results.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked (AQA required practical). Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: connect the wire to a battery/power pack in series with an ammeter (and a switch); connect a voltmeter in parallel across the length of wire being tested; tape the wire to a metre ruler and use a crocodile clip to choose the length; start at e.g. 10 cm and increase in steps of 10 cm up to 100 cm; read the current and potential difference for each length; calculate resistance R = V ÷ I; repeat and take a mean; control variables: same wire material and thickness, same potential difference, same temperature; switch off between readings so the wire does not heat up (heating raises resistance / safety: wire can get hot); plot a graph of resistance against length; expect a straight line through the origin: resistance is directly proportional to length.

questions.q:
An LDR (light-dependent resistor) is used in a circuit that switches on a street lamp.
Explain how the resistance of the LDR and the current through it change when it gets dark.
questions.ms: B1: when it gets dark the light intensity falls, so the resistance of the LDR increases. B1: the current through the LDR decreases (for the same potential difference). B1: this change is used to switch the lamp on at night / the LDR takes a bigger share of the potential difference.

questions.q:
Revisit (inheritance). In pea plants, the allele for tall plants (T) is dominant over the allele for short plants (t).
A Tt plant is crossed with a tt plant. Draw a Punnett square for this cross. Type the gametes of each parent and the genotypes of the four offspring.
questions.ms: B1: gametes T and t from the first parent, t and t from the second. B1: offspring Tt, Tt, tt, tt.

questions.q: What percentage of the offspring are expected to be short? (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 50%. B1 (2 out of 4 offspring are tt).

questions.q:
Revisit (reacting masses). Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide that can be made from 12 g of magnesium. (g)
questions.ms: Answer: 20 g. M1 for Mr of MgO = 24 + 16 = 40. M1 for 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol of Mg, which makes 0.5 mol of MgO (ratio 2 : 2), or 48 g Mg → 80 g MgO. A1 for 0.5 × 40 = 20 g.

questions.q: A student only collects 16 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 80%. M1 for 16 ÷ 20 × 100. A1 for 80%. Follow through from their answer to 17a.
